questions.stem: A client sends three DHCPDISCOVER messages without an offer. Which behavior should smart relay enter next?

options.text: FortiGate forwards using the secondary IP relay targets and the secondary address as source.
options.feedback: The unanswered-request threshold has been reached; the source identity changes for the next relay phase.

options.text: FortiGate broadcasts the same request to every primary and secondary relay simultaneously.
options.feedback: That describes parallel relay fan-out, not smart relay's sequential source-identity fallback.

options.text: FortiGate disables DHCP relay until an administrator clears the client counter.
options.feedback: Smart relay is an automatic retry mechanism; it does not require a manual reset after the threshold.

options.text: FortiGate changes the client VLAN and restarts DHCP with a new subnet.
options.feedback: The feature changes relay source identity and target, not the access VLAN or client subnet.

questions.stem: A debug trace shows requests forwarded from the secondary interface address, but no DHCPOFFER arrives. What is proven?

options.text: The DHCP server selected the correct scope and reserved a lease for the client.
options.feedback: A server offer or acknowledgement is needed to prove the server processed the request.

options.text: The secondary fallback path was entered and FortiGate attempted to forward the request.
options.feedback: The changed source proves the retry phase; it does not prove the DHCP server accepted the scope request.

options.text: The client received an address and completed the DHCP four-message exchange.
options.feedback: Forwarding is not the same as receiving an offer and acknowledgement at the client.

options.text: The secondary relay address has no route because the source address changed.
options.feedback: The trace proves a forwarding attempt; inspect route lookup and return traffic before diagnosing reachability.

questions.stem: Which command is the documented application-level diagnostic for the relay transaction sequence?

options.text: diagnose debug application dnsproxy -1
options.feedback: DNS proxy diagnostics do not expose the DHCP relay transaction path.

options.text: diagnose debug application wad -1
options.feedback: WAD is the web proxy daemon, not the DHCP relay process.

options.text: diagnose debug application dhcprelay -1
options.feedback: The dhcprelay application debug exposes transaction IDs, request receipt, relay source and forwarding decisions.

options.text: diagnose debug application ike -1
options.feedback: IKE debugging concerns IPsec negotiation rather than DHCP relay.

questions.stem: After three unanswered requests in the secondary phase, what should the documented state machine do?

options.text: Continue using the secondary source indefinitely until a DHCPACK arrives.
options.feedback: The guide explicitly describes returning to the primary phase after three unanswered secondary requests.

options.text: Send the request to both relay identities in a single packet.
options.feedback: The feature does not define simultaneous primary/secondary relay fan-out.

options.text: Delete the secondary IP configuration and disable smart relay.
options.feedback: No configuration is removed; the retry sequence restarts with the primary identity.

options.text: Return to the primary relay identity and restart the unanswered-request sequence.
options.feedback: The documented fallback cycles back to primary after another three unanswered requests.

questions.stem: A device belongs to a group with value SITE-A but has a direct mapping SITE-B. Which value should the device receive?

options.text: The per-device value SITE-B overrides the device-group mapping.
options.feedback: FortiManager applies the more specific per-device mapping when one exists.

options.text: The group value SITE-A always wins over any device-specific value.
options.feedback: That reverses the documented precedence of a device-specific mapping.

options.text: The ADOM default is used whenever both group and device mappings exist.
options.feedback: The default is fallback when an applicable mapping is unavailable, not a higher-priority value.

options.text: The variable is undefined because group and device mappings conflict.
options.feedback: The mappings are designed to coexist; the direct device value is the specific override.

questions.stem: Which mapping scope is unavailable in the Global Database ADOM?

options.text: Default values are unavailable in the Global Database ADOM.
options.feedback: Default values are part of the variable definition and are not excluded by that limitation.

options.text: Per-device mapping is unavailable in the Global Database ADOM.
options.feedback: The guide distinguishes Global Database per-ADOM mapping from ordinary ADOM per-device mapping.

options.text: Per-ADOM mapping is unavailable in the Global Database ADOM.
options.feedback: The guide specifically makes per-ADOM mapping available in the Global Database ADOM.

options.text: Variable import and export are unavailable in every ADOM.
options.feedback: The guide documents JSON and CSV import/export of metadata variables.

questions.stem: A template contains $site_subnet but install preview still shows the literal token. What should be checked first?

options.text: Increase the variable value length beyond 32768 characters.
options.feedback: The documented maximum is 32768 characters; length does not explain literal substitution.

options.text: Convert the variable into a firewall address object before template rendering.
options.feedback: Variables can be used in supported objects and templates; conversion is not the first diagnostic step.

options.text: Confirm the field supports metadata variables and the target has an applicable mapping.
options.feedback: Variable expansion is field-specific and mapping-dependent; a variable definition alone is insufficient.

options.text: Disable the ADOM database and recreate the managed device.
options.feedback: That is destructive and unrelated to checking field eligibility and mapping resolution.

questions.stem: A DELETE request returns a reference-in-use error. What is the safest next action?

options.text: Repeat DELETE with a different request ID until it succeeds.
options.feedback: A new request ID does not remove the underlying reference dependency.

options.text: Change the variable type from normal to password and retry.
options.feedback: Changing type does not resolve an object or template reference.

options.text: Delete the entire ADOM to clear the metadata reference.
options.feedback: Deleting the ADOM is disproportionate and not the documented remediation.

options.text: Find objects or templates referencing the variable, remove dependencies, then retry deletion.
options.feedback: The API tip notes that a used variable must be checked for references before deletion.

questions.stem: A DR FortiAnalyzer must receive a once-daily incremental copy from a collector. Which mode fits?

options.text: Aggregation mode between the two FortiAnalyzer units.
options.feedback: Aggregation is designed for scheduled FAZ-to-FAZ transfer and avoids retransmitting logs already present.

options.text: Forwarding mode to a CEF destination with a daily schedule.
options.feedback: Forwarding and CEF are different destination/transfer semantics; aggregation is FAZ-to-FAZ only.

options.text: Syslog output with a local archive retention rule.
options.feedback: Syslog output does not provide the FAZ aggregation transaction or deduplication behavior.

options.text: Event-handler automation that exports only incident records.
options.feedback: Event handlers automate responses; they do not replicate the collected log archive.

questions.stem: Which receiver-side setting must be enabled before a client can aggregate logs to it?

options.text: set log-forward enable under config system global.
options.feedback: That is not the documented aggregation acceptance control.

options.text: set accept-aggregation enable under config system log-forward-service.
options.feedback: The receiver must explicitly accept aggregation before the client transfer can complete.

options.text: set mode aggregation under config system log-forward on the receiver.
options.feedback: The mode is configured on the client; the receiver enables the aggregation service.

options.text: set reliable enable under config system syslog.
options.feedback: Reliable syslog is not the FAZ aggregation service.

questions.stem: Which command can trigger an immediate aggregation test without waiting for the daily hour?

options.text: execute log-forward flush <id>
options.feedback: That is not the documented aggregation test command.

options.text: diagnose test application oftpd 99
options.feedback: Restarting a service does not prove or initiate the intended aggregation job.

options.text: execute log-aggregation <id>
options.feedback: The command runs the selected client log-forward aggregation ID immediately.

options.text: execute log backup all
options.feedback: A local backup is not the same as client-to-server aggregation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes duplicate handling in aggregation mode?

options.text: The receiver accepts every log again and relies on a report filter to hide duplicates.
options.feedback: Deduplication is part of the aggregation transfer behavior, not merely a report filter.

options.text: The client sends only logs that match a configured log filter.
options.feedback: Aggregation mode does not support log filters.

options.text: The client deletes local logs immediately after sending them.
options.feedback: The mode forwards collected logs; it does not define immediate local deletion.

options.text: The client sends logs not already present on the receiving FortiAnalyzer.
options.feedback: The guide describes incremental transfer to avoid duplicating records already on the server.

questions.stem: A host-facing access port emits an IPv6 Router Advertisement. What should a host-role RA-guard policy do?

options.text: Drop all RAs received from the host-role device.
options.feedback: The guide states that if the device is a host, all RA messages are dropped.

options.text: Forward the RA if the M flag is set.
options.feedback: The host-role rule drops all RAs before treating the host as a router.

options.text: Forward the RA only when its router preference is high.
options.feedback: A host should not be advertising router information regardless of preference.

options.text: Convert the RA into a DHCPv6 relay request.
options.feedback: RA Guard filters RAs; it does not translate them into DHCPv6 messages.

questions.stem: Which object constrains the IPv6 prefix advertised inside an RA?

options.text: An IPv6 access list matching the source link-local address.
options.feedback: The access list constrains source addresses, not the advertised prefix.

options.text: An IPv6 prefix list referenced by the RA-guard policy.
options.feedback: The prefix list checks the prefix in the RA Prefix Information option.

options.text: A DHCP snooping binding database.
options.feedback: DHCP snooping bindings track address leases and are not the RA prefix policy object.

options.text: An SD-WAN route-tag address object.
options.feedback: Route-tag objects are unrelated to IPv6 RA inspection.

questions.stem: A legitimate router's RA is dropped even though its prefix is correct. Which policy input is worth checking next?

options.text: The FortiSwitch PoE budget and LLDP power allocation.
options.feedback: Power allocation does not affect RA Guard policy matching.

options.text: The FortiGate DHCP relay server list.
options.feedback: DHCP relay is a different control plane from IPv6 RA filtering.

options.text: The source IPv6 access list, hop-limit range, flags and router preference.
options.feedback: RA Guard evaluates multiple criteria; a correct prefix alone is not sufficient.

options.text: The FortiSwitch MCLAG priority and ICL state.
options.feedback: MCLAG split-brain settings do not determine RA policy criteria.

questions.stem: The RA-guard policy exists and is correct, but rogue RAs still reach clients. What configuration gap is most likely?

options.text: The IPv6 prefix list is stored in the wrong ADOM.
options.feedback: FortiSwitch RA Guard is not managed through FortiManager ADOM metadata scope.

options.text: The switch has not received an sFlow collector template.
options.feedback: sFlow is telemetry export and does not activate RA Guard.

options.text: The router has not sent a DHCPACK for the host.
options.feedback: RA Guard enforcement does not depend on DHCP lease acknowledgement.

options.text: The policy is not bound to the ingress interface and VLAN carrying the rogue RA.
options.feedback: A policy object does not enforce until it is applied to the relevant port/VLAN.

questions.stem: What is the primary role of 802.11k assisted roaming in the FortiAP SSID options?

options.text: Provide neighboring-AP information so the client can evaluate roam candidates more efficiently.
options.feedback: 802.11k supplies neighbor/site information; the client still makes the roam decision.

options.text: Force the client to reassociate to the AP with the lowest channel utilization.
options.feedback: That describes steering pressure, not the neighbor-information function of 802.11k.

options.text: Encrypt the backhaul between a mesh root and leaf AP.
options.feedback: Mesh backhaul protection is unrelated to 802.11k neighbor reports.

options.text: Replace RADIUS authentication with cached PMK material.
options.feedback: 802.11k does not replace the authentication method.

questions.stem: A client remains on a congested AP while a nearby AP has better RSSI. Which setting is intended to assist?

options.text: 802.11k alone, because neighbor information forces a roam.
options.feedback: Neighbor information assists client choice but does not force reassociation.

options.text: 802.11v assisted roaming, subject to client behavior and the Fortinet implementation.
options.feedback: Fortinet documents 802.11v as helping clients move from congested APs when a better AP is available.

options.text: 802.11r, because Fast BSS Transition chooses the least-congested AP.
options.feedback: 802.11r reduces transition authentication delay; it is not the steering decision mechanism.

options.text: WIDS rogue AP detection, because it measures RSSI for all clients.
options.feedback: WIDS is intrusion detection and does not provide the documented assisted-roaming function.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes 802.11r from 802.11k neighbor assistance?

options.text: 802.11r chooses the best AP, while 802.11k encrypts the reassociation frame.
options.feedback: That reverses their functions and assigns an encryption role to 802.11k.

options.text: 802.11r is the RADIUS attribute carrying the SSID to FortiNAC.
options.feedback: RADIUS Attribute 30 is a separate identity-context requirement for FortiNAC auto-registration.

options.text: 802.11r accelerates transition authentication; 802.11k supplies neighboring-AP information.
options.feedback: The protocols address different stages of roaming and can be configured separately.

options.text: 802.11r controls radio background scan intervals, while 802.11k controls channel power.
options.feedback: Those are not the documented functions of the roaming protocols.

questions.stem: A profile rejects an eighth SSID while background scanning is enabled. What trade-off should be evaluated?

options.text: Increase the RADIUS server's maximum concurrent authentications.
options.feedback: The reported limit is a FortiAP profile VAP capacity constraint, not a RADIUS session limit.

options.text: Convert the SSID to a FortiNAC registration VLAN.
options.feedback: VLAN role does not change the FortiAP per-radio VAP limit.

options.text: Enable MLO on the radio to increase the VAP count automatically.
options.feedback: Multi-Link Operation does not override the documented background-scan VAP constraint.

options.text: The documented seven-VAP limit with scanning versus eight when scanning is disabled.
options.feedback: The Community tip describes this capacity interaction; disabling roaming assistance may remove mobility benefits.

questions.stem: Which RADIUS attribute must carry the SSID value for FortiNAC per-SSID Dot1x Auto Registration?

options.text: Attribute 30, Called-Station-Id, with the SSID value included.
options.feedback: The FortiNAC guide explicitly requires RADIUS Attribute 30 to include the SSID value.

options.text: Attribute 1, User-Name, containing the employee's login name.
options.feedback: User-Name identifies the authenticated identity, not the SSID context required by the feature.

options.text: Attribute 8, Framed-IP-Address, containing the assigned client address.
options.feedback: The assigned IP address is not the SSID identifier used by auto-registration.

options.text: Attribute 26, Vendor-Specific, containing the FortiAP serial number.
options.feedback: The documented requirement is Attribute 30 with the SSID value.

questions.stem: After successful 802.1X authentication, when does FortiNAC perform the automatic host-user registration?

options.text: Only after the host receives its final production VLAN.
options.feedback: That would place registration after the policy decision, contrary to the documented order.

options.text: Before the network access policy is determined.
options.feedback: The guide specifies that host registration to the authenticated user occurs before policy determination.

options.text: Before the RADIUS Access-Request reaches the authentication server.
options.feedback: The feature depends on successful 802.1X authentication first.

options.text: Only after the endpoint completes a compliance scan.
options.feedback: Compliance scanning is a separate host-state/policy input.

questions.stem: A RADIUS Access-Accept is observed, but the endpoint remains unregistered. What evidence should be checked next?

options.text: The FortiSwitch PoE power consumption for the AP port.
options.feedback: PoE telemetry does not prove RADIUS SSID context or host registration.

options.text: The FortiAnalyzer aggregation schedule for the wireless logs.
options.feedback: Log forwarding does not create the host-user association.

options.text: The request's Attribute 30 SSID value and the FortiNAC host-user association.
options.feedback: Authentication success does not prove that the SSID auto-registration step occurred.

options.text: The FortiGate BGP route tag for the wireless subnet.
options.feedback: Route tags affect SD-WAN route matching, not FortiNAC registration.

questions.stem: Dot1x Auto Registration is enabled on one SSID, but not another. What should be expected?

options.text: Every SSID on the controller inherits the setting automatically.
options.feedback: The guide describes the setting per SSID, not as a controller-wide default.

options.text: All RADIUS users are registered regardless of SSID value.
options.feedback: The feature requires the SSID value in Attribute 30.

options.text: The setting applies only to wired switch ports.
options.feedback: The source feature is explicitly part of SSID configuration.

options.text: Only requests mapped to the enabled SSID and carrying its Attribute 30 value use the feature.
options.feedback: The setting is per SSID, and the request must identify the corresponding SSID.

questions.stem: In FortiNAC-F N+1 failover, who performs the primary CA health checks?

options.text: The secondary CA performs direct and indirect checks; FortiNAC-M manages the group.
options.feedback: The guide states that health checks are performed by the secondary, not the Manager.

options.text: FortiNAC-M performs every health check and commands promotion.
options.feedback: FortiNAC-M manages group visibility, but the secondary makes the health-check decision.

options.text: Each primary checks itself and votes with the Manager.
options.feedback: The documented direct/indirect checks originate from the secondary CA.

options.text: The FortiGate gateway performs the checks and triggers the CA promotion.
options.feedback: The 7.6.3 refinement removes the need for gateway-check logic.

questions.stem: The secondary cannot reach Primary A directly, but Primary B can reach A and reports it healthy. What should happen?

options.text: The secondary must promote immediately after any direct-check failure.
options.feedback: Promotion requires both direct and indirect checks to fail.

options.text: Failover should not be triggered because the indirect health check succeeds.
options.feedback: The indirect check prevents a false promotion caused by one failed network path.

options.text: Primary B should be promoted instead of the standby secondary.
options.feedback: Primary B is used as an indirect checker, not as the standby takeover node.

options.text: The Manager should remove Primary A from the N+1 group automatically.
options.feedback: A successful indirect check is evidence that the primary remains reachable.

questions.stem: Which health-check types remain in the FortiNAC-F 7.6.3 refinement?

options.text: RADIUS and TCP echo only.
options.feedback: Those are the two check types the 7.6.3 refinement removes.

options.text: HTTP and DNS application checks.
options.feedback: The release note identifies ICMP and TCP on a specific port, not HTTP/DNS.

options.text: ICMP and TCP on a specific port.
options.feedback: The 7.6.3 release notes state that RADIUS and TCP echo were removed from the custom check types.

options.text: SNMP polling and LDAP bind checks.
options.feedback: Those are not the retained N+1 health-check types.

questions.stem: A failed primary returns online after the secondary is promoted. What restores the original role arrangement?

options.text: Wait for automatic preemption as soon as the primary pings.
options.feedback: The documented recovery process requires manual reactivation of the primary.

options.text: Delete and recreate the N+1 group to force the primary active.
options.feedback: Recreating the group is not the documented recovery action.

options.text: Reboot the Manager so it elects the original primary.
options.feedback: The Manager does not perform the health-check election.

options.text: Manually use Resume Control on the primary/secondary workflow and verify statuses.
options.feedback: The guide states the recovered primary remains Standby until an administrator resumes control.

questions.stem: A user authenticates to the IdP but one application tile is hidden. What is the first policy object to inspect?

options.text: The SAML service provider's remote LDAP group filter and subtype.
options.feedback: Per-SP authorization hides applications when the user fails that SP's group filter.

options.text: The user's password policy and local password expiry.
options.feedback: Successful IdP authentication already occurred; the failure is per-SP authorization.

options.text: The SP's TLS cipher preference and server certificate chain.
options.feedback: Those may affect assertion transport/trust, but do not explain a group-filtered portal tile.

options.text: The FortiAuthenticator REST API local-user endpoint.
options.feedback: Local-user CRUD is separate from SAML SP authorization.

questions.stem: Which subtype performs a custom LDAP query that returns the member users?

options.text: LDAP directory group.
options.feedback: That maps to a group object at a specified distinguished name.

options.text: LDAP filter (advanced).
options.feedback: The guide defines this subtype as a custom filter query against the remote LDAP server.

options.text: List of users.
options.feedback: That is an explicit user-list source, not a dynamic LDAP query.

options.text: Global Authorization.
options.feedback: That is the renamed column for user-source authorization, not a filter subtype.

questions.stem: What does FortiAuthenticator do when a user fails a particular SP group filter in the IdP-initiated portal?

options.text: It disables the user's entire SAML account across every service provider.
options.feedback: The filter is per SP, so other authorized applications can remain available.

options.text: It sends an empty assertion to the SP and lets the SP decide.
options.feedback: The documented portal behavior is to hide the unauthorized SP.

options.text: It hides that SP from the portal and can log the authorization denial.
options.feedback: The 8.0 feature hides unauthorized SPs and records filter-denial events.

options.text: It changes the user's LDAP group membership automatically.
options.feedback: The feature evaluates membership; it does not rewrite the directory.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates IdP authentication from per-SP authorization?

options.text: Successful IdP login automatically authorizes every configured SP.
options.feedback: Per-SP authorization exists specifically to restrict individual service providers.

options.text: The SP group filter validates the user's password against LDAP.
options.feedback: The password is part of authentication; the filter determines group-based SP access.

options.text: A hidden SP proves the SAML signing certificate is expired.
options.feedback: A hidden tile can result from group-filter denial, not necessarily certificate failure.

options.text: Successful IdP login proves identity authentication, while each SP group filter makes a separate access decision.
options.feedback: The 8.0 enhancement adds an authorization check after the user authenticates to the IdP.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of approval tiers supported by a FortiPAM approval profile?

options.text: Three tiers, each with its own required approvals and reviewer users/groups.
options.feedback: The FortiPAM 1.9 guide documents up to three approval tiers.

options.text: One tier with an unlimited number of parallel reviewers.
options.feedback: The product supports multiple sequential tiers, up to three.

options.text: Five tiers, each requiring one administrator approval.
options.feedback: The documented maximum is three tiers, not five.

options.text: Two tiers that can only contain local users.
options.feedback: Each tier can include users and user groups; the limit is three.

questions.stem: A request is approved but no launcher starts automatically. Which setting explains this?

options.text: The approver has not changed the request timezone.
options.feedback: Timezone display does not control whether a secret launches automatically.

options.text: Start Upon Approval is disabled, which is the default.
options.feedback: Approval and automatic launch are separate; the default does not auto-start the secret.

options.text: The secret's password verification interval has expired.
options.feedback: Password verification is a separate secret-maintenance workflow.

options.text: The request type was Launcher rather than Job.
options.feedback: Both Launcher and Job requests can use approval; Start Upon Approval controls automatic launch.

questions.stem: An approver revokes an approval after the requester has launched the secret. What happens?

options.text: The session continues until the originally approved end time.
options.feedback: Revocation is immediate and terminates an already launched session.

options.text: Only future requests are denied; the current request remains approved.
options.feedback: The current approval is revoked and the request must be approved again.

options.text: The active secret session is immediately terminated and the request resets.
options.feedback: The approval guide explicitly describes session termination and request reset after revocation.

options.text: The secret password is automatically rotated before the session ends.
options.feedback: Revocation terminates access; it does not define a password-change action.

questions.stem: Which request type is tied to a job whose secret has Requires Approval to Launch Job enabled?

options.text: Launcher request; the requester manually selects an unrelated secret.
options.feedback: Launcher requests select secrets; Job requests bind to the job's associated secret.

options.text: Session recording request; the secret is selected from the audit log.
options.feedback: Session recording is a secret setting, not an approval request type.

options.text: Password verification request; the password changer creates the request.
options.feedback: Password verification is separate from the approval workflow.

options.text: Job request; the job's associated secret is selected automatically.
options.feedback: The Make a Request guide distinguishes Launcher and Job requests and their secret linkage.

questions.stem: A rule should count distinct destination IPs separately for each source. Which Group By key is essential?

options.text: Source IP, so each source has an independent aggregate bucket.
options.feedback: Grouping by source separates one host's behavior from every other host.

options.text: Event Receive Time only, so all sources share one time bucket.
options.feedback: That groups by time rather than actor and can combine unrelated sources.

options.text: Destination IP, so each destination is counted as a separate source.
options.feedback: That reverses the intended actor/destination relationship.

options.text: Incident Status, so open incidents are counted separately.
options.feedback: Incident status is not the source identity used for the event aggregation.

questions.stem: Which expression detects at least 100 distinct destination IPs from the same source?

options.text: COUNT(Destination IP) >= 100 with no grouping.
options.feedback: That can count repeated events and combine multiple source hosts.

options.text: COUNT(DISTINCT Destination IP) >= 100 grouped by Source IP.
options.feedback: Distinct count avoids counting repeated connections to the same destination as new destinations.

options.text: SUM(Destination IP) >= 100 grouped by destination port.
options.feedback: IP addresses are not summed as a meaningful scan threshold.

options.text: MAX(Destination IP) >= 100 grouped by Event Type.
options.feedback: A maximum value does not measure the number of distinct destinations.

questions.stem: A scheduled rule on a non-ClickHouse deployment needs two subpatterns with FOLLOWED_BY. What limitation applies?

options.text: All scheduled rules support unlimited subpatterns on every engine.
options.feedback: The multiple-subpattern sequence behavior is engine-dependent.

options.text: FOLLOWED_BY is supported only by streaming rules on non-ClickHouse.
options.feedback: The documented exception specifically allows ClickHouse scheduled rules with Multiple Subpatterns.

options.text: Non-ClickHouse scheduled rules allow only one subpattern.
options.feedback: The 7.4 guide documents the one-subpattern limit for scheduled rules in non-ClickHouse environments.

options.text: The rule must be converted into an event handler in FortiAnalyzer.
options.feedback: That is a different product and does not change FortiSIEM engine limits.

questions.stem: A rule fires but the incident does not identify the source host. What should be reviewed?

options.text: Increase the aggregate threshold so the source is included automatically.
options.feedback: Threshold changes do not populate missing incident attributes.

options.text: Change the event parser to emit the incident ID as Source IP.
options.feedback: That would corrupt event semantics and does not map the grouped value.

options.text: Disable the clear condition so the source stays visible.
options.feedback: Clear conditions do not populate incident fields.

options.text: Map the subpattern's Group By source attribute into the incident attributes.
options.feedback: The incident definition should carry the group values that identify the triggering cohort.

questions.stem: Which path does the main FortiSASE DEM SaaS application dashboard measure?

options.text: The first-mile path from provisioned FortiSASE PoPs to the SaaS applications.
options.feedback: The main dashboard reports health-check metrics between PoPs and SaaS endpoints.

options.text: The user's Wi-Fi radio to the local access switch.
options.feedback: That is a local LAN segment, not the PoP-to-SaaS measurement.

options.text: The endpoint's TCP path to the PoP underlay only.
options.feedback: That is the separate managed-endpoint Network Metrics view.

options.text: The SaaS application's internal database query time.
options.feedback: The documented metric is network health to the application, not its internal transaction latency.

questions.stem: Which endpoint state is required for the documented TCP latency chart?

options.text: The endpoint is unmanaged but has a browser session to the portal.
options.feedback: A browser login does not substitute for endpoint management and the DEM agent.

options.text: The endpoint is managed through an invitation code and its DEM agent is Online.
options.feedback: The guide lists an active management connection and Online DEM agent as prerequisites.

options.text: The endpoint is offline but has a cached certificate.
options.feedback: The agent must be Online to provide endpoint metrics.

options.text: The endpoint has a FortiGate DHCP lease but no DEM agent.
options.feedback: A DHCP lease does not provide the endpoint measurement agent.

questions.stem: Why add an FQDN steering bypass for the FortiSASE Turbo URL on tunnel-connected Windows endpoints?

options.text: To bypass all security inspection for every SaaS application.
options.feedback: The documented bypass is specific to the Turbo URL measurement path.

options.text: To force the endpoint to use a different SaaS application catalogue.
options.feedback: The bypass affects measurement routing, not application discovery.

options.text: To keep the TCP latency measurement on the underlay path to the PoP.
options.feedback: The bypass prevents the tunnel from obscuring the intended underlay measurement.

options.text: To make the DEM agent report only the tunnel's encrypted packet size.
options.feedback: The purpose is to measure underlay TCP latency, not packet size.

questions.stem: Zoom and Teams are missing from a DEM dashboard in the Mature version. What does the cited Community tip identify?

options.text: A local firewall policy is blocking the endpoint's DNS queries.
options.feedback: The cited case was resolved by moving to the Feature version, not a local policy change.

options.text: The DEM agent must be reinstalled on every endpoint.
options.feedback: The issue was application visibility in the dashboard, not agent installation.

options.text: The PoP health-check history must be cleared before applications appear.
options.feedback: The tip identifies version channel, not stale metric history.

options.text: The Feature version displays them after an upgrade from the Mature version.
options.feedback: The 2025 tip documents a release-channel application-list difference.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between a BGP community and a FortiGate route tag?

options.text: The route map matches the received community and assigns a local route tag for SD-WAN matching.
options.feedback: The community is carried with BGP; the FortiGate route tag is local metadata set by policy.

options.text: The route tag is a standard BGP path attribute advertised unchanged to every peer.
options.feedback: The documentation distinguishes local route tags from BGP communities.

options.text: The BGP community is inserted by the SD-WAN service after path selection.
options.feedback: The community arrives with the BGP route; the inbound route map translates it.

options.text: The route tag is the same as an IPv4 destination prefix.
options.feedback: A route tag labels a set of learned routes; it is not a prefix.

questions.stem: A BGP community is received correctly but the learned route has no tag. Which attachment is most important?

options.text: Attach the route map outbound on the neighbor only.
options.feedback: An outbound route map does not tag the routes learned from that peer.

options.text: Attach the community-matching route map inbound on the neighbor.
options.feedback: The route map must process received routes to assign the local route tag.

options.text: Attach the route map to the SD-WAN service instead of BGP.
options.feedback: The tag is assigned during BGP route processing before SD-WAN matches it.

options.text: Attach the route map to a firewall policy after NAT.
options.feedback: Firewall policy evaluation does not assign the BGP route tag.

questions.stem: In FortiOS 7.4.5, how is a tagged BGP destination referenced by an SD-WAN service?

options.text: Create a normal subnet address for every learned prefix manually.
options.feedback: The purpose is to avoid hard-coding dynamic prefixes one by one.

options.text: Use the BGP community string directly as an IP address object.
options.feedback: A community is not a destination subnet and is translated to a route tag.

options.text: Create a firewall address object of type route-tag and use it as the service destination.
options.feedback: The 7.4.5 guide documents route-tag address objects for SD-WAN destination matching.

options.text: Create an ISDB custom application signature for the route tag.
options.feedback: ISDB application matching is unrelated to BGP route-tag destination objects.

questions.stem: Which pair of checks best separates tag assignment from SD-WAN member selection?

options.text: Check only the firewall policy hit counter and assume the route tag matched.
options.feedback: A policy hit does not prove the intended SD-WAN rule or member selection.

options.text: Check only the BGP neighbor state and assume every prefix is tagged.
options.feedback: An established neighbor does not prove route-map matching or tag assignment.

options.text: Check only interface link status and assume the dynamic destination is correct.
options.feedback: Link state does not prove the BGP tag or service destination match.

options.text: Inspect the BGP table's RouteTag field, then inspect the SD-WAN service's selected members.
options.feedback: The BGP table proves tag assignment; the SD-WAN service diagnostic proves rule/member selection.

questions.stem: A FortiManager variable is mapped and a FortiAnalyzer aggregation job is configured. Which evidence proves each runtime outcome?

options.text: Rendered install preview proves variable resolution; destination Log View proves transferred logs were indexed.
options.feedback: The two checks validate different runtime stages rather than relying on configuration presence alone.

options.text: The variable list and log-forward ID list prove both outcomes completely.
options.feedback: Those views prove configuration objects exist, not that values rendered or logs arrived.

options.text: The FortiManager device online flag and FortiAnalyzer disk quota prove both outcomes.
options.feedback: Device reachability and quota are prerequisites, not end-to-end success evidence.

options.text: A single ping to both appliances proves both workflows completed.
options.feedback: ICMP reachability does not validate template substitution or log transfer/indexing.

questions.stem: A user passes 802.1X but is not auto-registered in FortiNAC; another user authenticates to FortiAuthenticator but cannot see an SP. What is common?

options.text: Both failures are caused by an expired TLS certificate on the access point.
options.feedback: The two symptoms involve distinct post-authentication policy inputs.

options.text: Authentication succeeded, but a separate context/authorization step still needs verification.
options.feedback: Both workflows have a post-authentication decision that can fail independently of credential validation.

options.text: Both products require the same RADIUS Attribute 30 value for every SAML SP.
options.feedback: Attribute 30 is the FortiNAC SSID requirement, not a universal SAML authorization input.

options.text: Successful authentication guarantees every downstream access decision.
options.feedback: Both examples demonstrate that authentication and authorization/registration are separate.
